rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem:
Complete and balance the following chemical equations :
(a) \(\mathrm{8MnO_4^{-} + 3S_2O_3^{2-} + H_2O} \longrightarrow\)
(b) \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 3\ Sn^{2+} + 14H^{+}} \longrightarrow\)
rows.solution:
(a) In neutral or faintly alkaline solution permanganate is reduced only as far as manganese dioxide, while thiosulphate is oxidised all the way to sulphate:
\(8\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 3\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow 8\mathrm{MnO_2} + 6\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}} + 2\mathrm{OH^-}\)

The electron count confirms it: manganese goes from \(+7\) to \(+4\), three electrons each for eight atoms, twenty-four in all; and in each thiosulphate the two sulphurs go from an average \(+2\) to \(+6\), four electrons each, eight per ion and twenty-four for three ions.

(b) Acidified dichromate oxidises tin(II) to tin(IV) and is itself reduced to \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\):
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 3\mathrm{Sn^{2+}} + 14\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 3\mathrm{Sn^{4+}} + 7\mathrm{H_2O}\)
Here two chromiums take three electrons each and three tins give two each, so six electrons pass either way.

rows.stem:
What are the hydrolysis products of :
(a) Sucrose
(b) Lactose
rows.solution:
(a) Sucrose is a disaccharide of one glucose unit and one fructose unit, so hydrolysis gives D-(+)-glucose and D-(−)-fructose:
\(\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6} + \mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\)
The mixture is called invert sugar, because fructose is so strongly laevorotatory that the net rotation changes sign during the hydrolysis.

(b) Lactose is a disaccharide of one glucose unit and one galactose unit joined by a \(\beta\)-1,4 linkage, so hydrolysis gives D-(+)-glucose and D-(+)-galactose.

rows.stem: Henry's law constant for \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) in water is \(1.67 \times 10^8\) Pa at 298 K. Calculate the number of moles of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) in 500 ml of soda water when packed under \(2.53 \times 10^5\) Pa at the same temperature.
rows.solution:
Henry's law in the mole-fraction form gives the amount dissolved:
\(p = K_H\,x \implies x_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = \dfrac{p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}{K_H} = \dfrac{2.53 \times 10^{5}}{1.67 \times 10^{8}} = 1.51 \times 10^{-3}\)

Soda water is essentially water, so the moles of solvent are
\(n_{\mathrm{H_2O}} = \dfrac{500}{18} = 27.78\ \mathrm{mol}\)
taking the density of water as 1 g \(\mathrm{mL^{-1}}\), so that 500 mL is 500 g.

Because the solution is very dilute, the mole fraction of the gas may be taken as \(n_{\mathrm{CO_2}}/n_{\mathrm{H_2O}}\):
\(n_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 27.78 \times 1.51 \times 10^{-3} = 42.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}\)

So about \(0.042\) mol of carbon dioxide. Both pressures are in the same unit, pascals, so no conversion is needed and the mole fraction comes out dimensionless, as it must.

rows.stem:
Calculate \(\Delta_r G^{\circ}\) and log \(\mathrm{K_C}\) of the reaction.
\(\mathrm{2Cr(s) + 3Cd^{2+}(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{2Cr^{3+}(aq) + 3Cd(s)}\)
Given \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Cr^{3+}/Cr}} = -0.74\) V
\(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Cd^{2+}/Cd}} = -0.40\) V
[R = 8.314 J \(\mathrm{K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\), F = 96500 C \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)]
rows.solution:
The cadmium couple has the higher reduction potential, so it is the cathode:
\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cd^{2+}/Cd}} - E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cr^{3+}/Cr}} = (-0.40) - (-0.74) = +0.34\ \mathrm{V}\)

Two chromium atoms give up three electrons each, so six electrons are transferred and \(n = 6\):
\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}_{cell} = -(6 \times 96500 \times 0.34) = -196860\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\)
that is \(-196.86\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\).

The equilibrium constant follows:
\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -2.303\,RT\log K_C\)
\(\log K_C = \dfrac{196860}{2.303 \times 8.314 \times 298} = 34.576\)

Note how much the value of \(n\) matters here: the same \(0.34\) V with \(n = 1\) would give \(\log K_C\) near 5.8, not 34.6. The number of electrons must come from the BALANCED equation.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
The rate of a reaction quadruples when the temperature changes from 293 K to 313 K. Calculate the energy of activation of the reaction assuming that it does not change with temperature.
[Given : log 4 = 0.602, log 2 = 0.301, R = 8.314 J \(\mathrm{K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\)]
rows.solution:
Use the two-temperature form of the Arrhenius equation:
\(\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\left[\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1 T_2}\right]\)

The rate quadruples, so \(k_2/k_1 = 4\) and the left side is \(\log 4 = 0.602\). With \(T_1 = 293\) K and \(T_2 = 313\) K,
\(0.602 = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303 \times 8.314} \times \dfrac{20}{313 \times 293} = \dfrac{E_a}{19.147} \times \dfrac{20}{313 \times 293}\)

\(E_a = \dfrac{0.602 \times 19.147 \times 313 \times 293}{20}\)
\(E_a = 52850\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\), that is \(52.85\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

The question supplies \(\log 2\) as well as \(\log 4\), but only \(\log 4\) is needed; \(\log 2\) would serve if the ratio were worked out as \(2 \log 2\).

rows.stem:
Define the following terms :
(a) Native protein
(b) Nucleotide
(c) Essential amino acid
rows.solution:
(a) A native protein is a protein as it exists in a biological system: its unique three-dimensional structure — the secondary and tertiary folding — is intact, and it is biologically active. Destroy that folding by heat or a change in pH and the protein is denatured, losing its activity although its primary sequence survives.

(b) A nucleotide is the repeating unit of a nucleic acid, made of three components joined together: a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate group. Equivalently, it is what forms when a nucleoside — base plus sugar — is linked to phosphoric acid.

(c) An essential amino acid is one the body cannot synthesise for itself and which must therefore be obtained ready-made from the diet. Valine, leucine and lysine are examples. Those the body can synthesise are called non-essential.

rows.stem:
In the following complex ions, explain the type of hybridisation, shape and magnetic property :
(a) \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{2+}}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}\)
(At. Nos. : Fe = 26, Ni = 28)
rows.solution:
(a) \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{2+}}\). Iron is \(+2\), so \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is \(3d^6\). Water is a WEAK field ligand, so the crystal field splitting is smaller than the pairing energy and the six d electrons spread out rather than pair — one orbital doubly occupied and four singly, leaving FOUR unpaired electrons. With every \(3d\) orbital occupied, none is free for bonding, so the complex must use outer orbitals.
Hybridisation: \(sp^3d^2\); shape: octahedral; magnetic property: paramagnetic, with four unpaired electrons.

(b) \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}\). Nickel is \(+2\), so \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\), which has two unpaired electrons. The chloride ion is a weak field ligand and cannot force them to pair, so the \(3d\) set is left as it is and bonding uses the \(4s\) and three \(4p\) orbitals.
Hybridisation: \(sp^3\); shape: tetrahedral; magnetic property: paramagnetic, with two unpaired electrons.

The contrast worth noting is with \(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}}\), where the strong field cyanide ligand pairs those two electrons, frees a \(3d\) orbital, and gives a \(dsp^2\) square planar diamagnetic complex from the same metal ion.

rows.stem:
(a) Write IUPAC names of the following :
(i) \(\mathrm{[Co(H_2O)(CN)(en)_2]^{2+}}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{[PtCl_4]^{2-}}\)
(iii) \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_4Cl(ONO)]^{+}}\)
(b) What is spectrochemical series ? Write the difference between a strong field ligand and a weak field ligand.
rows.solution:
(a)(i) The ion carries \(+2\). Inside it the aqua ligand and the two ethane-1,2-diamine ligands are neutral and the cyanido ligand is \(-1\), so cobalt is \(+3\). Ligands are cited alphabetically — aqua, cyanido, ethane-1,2-diamine — and the last takes the prefix bis because its own name contains numerals:
aquacyanidobis(ethane-1,2-diamine)cobalt(III) ion

(ii) Four chlorido ligands contribute \(-4\) against an overall \(-2\), so platinum is \(+2\). The species is an anion, so platinum takes the \(-ate\) ending:
tetrachloridoplatinate(II) ion

(iii) Four neutral ammine ligands, one chlorido at \(-1\) and one nitrito at \(-1\) against an overall \(+1\) put chromium at \(+3\). The \(\mathrm{ONO}\) notation means the ambidentate nitrite ion is bound through OXYGEN, shown as nitrito-O:
tetraamminechloridonitrito-O-chromium(III) ion

(b) The spectrochemical series is the arrangement of ligands in order of increasing field strength — that is, in order of how large a crystal field splitting they produce. It is determined experimentally, from the light that complexes of different ligands absorb, and runs from weak field ligands such as \(\mathrm{I^-}\), \(\mathrm{Br^-}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\), through \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) and \(\mathrm{NH_3}\), to strong field ligands such as \(\mathrm{CN^-}\) and \(\mathrm{CO}\).

A WEAK field ligand produces a splitting smaller than the pairing energy, \(\Delta_0 < \mathrm{P}\). The electrons then prefer to occupy the upper set rather than pair, so the complex is HIGH SPIN with the maximum number of unpaired electrons.

A STRONG field ligand produces a splitting larger than the pairing energy, \(\Delta_0 > \mathrm{P}\). Pairing then costs less than promotion, so the electrons fill the lower set first and the complex is LOW SPIN, with fewer unpaired electrons and often diamagnetic.
